finding: Non-Goal 1 asserts "the three write defects are the only intentional behaviour changes in this release" and "every removal preserves observable behaviour". Three sections of the same spec contradict it: §9.1 changes an exit code from 1 to 2 (observable to any driver, and the exit-code table is a documented contract), §9.2 and §9.3 change the `hint` field of error output (observable in the agent-facing JSON contract), and §5 changes the quality gate command (observable at every close). A unit reading Non-Goal 1 as its scope fence and a unit implementing §9 are given opposite instructions about whether a behaviour change is in scope.

resolved.evidence: Non-Goal 1 now enumerates all five intentional behaviour changes and restricts the preservation clause to the sweeps in sections 6-8.

suggestion: Rewrite Non-Goal 1 to enumerate the actual intentional behaviour changes — the three write defects plus the §9 exit-code/hint changes and the §5 gate change — and restrict the preservation clause to the sweep sections (§6, §7, §8), which are the ones that must be behaviour-neutral.

finding: Item 11 ("Every guard test surviving §7 has a recorded mutation that makes it fail") is listed under Tests but is not a test: it quantifies over "the guard class", a set §7.1 defines only in prose ("tests written to prevent a specific defect from returning") with no marker, naming convention or manifest, and it names no artifact where the mutation is "recorded" (closure evidence? a comment at the test? a file?). Nothing in `go test ./...` can fail if the property is violated, and nothing lets a later reader or the v0.35.0 unattended loop verify it. Since §7's mutation criterion is the method that makes §2.1's test-removal contract meaningful, its only enforcement item is unenforceable — the same shape as the §2 problem, one level down.

resolved.evidence: Test item 11 replaced with a checkable oracle: the set of tests carrying a // guard: marker equals the surviving subset of the 7.1 list.

suggestion: Pin the artifact and the set: name where the mutation record lives (e.g. a one-line `// mutation: <what was broken> -> <test> fails` at each guard test, which also makes the guard class mechanically enumerable by that marker), and restate item 11 as a check over that marker set — e.g. a workflow `checks` entry asserting every test carrying the guard marker also carries a mutation record. If the record is only closure evidence, move item 11 out of §12 and into §7 as a process rule, so §12 contains only things that can fail.

finding: "repeated enough times to have caught the 1-in-20 failure" is not a pass criterion. Two engineers write N=20 and N=1000 and both claim compliance, and neither run proves anything: a probabilistic test that passes is consistent with the lost update still being possible (it only failed 1 run in 20 before). Worse, the test can only ever fail flakily, which is the property §7 is elsewhere removing from the suite.

resolved.evidence: Test item 1 is now deterministic: hold the write lock, start the second writer, release, assert both writers' tasks survive. No repeat count.

suggestion: Either pin the iteration count and the tolerated failure rate explicitly (e.g. "200 iterations, zero losses"), or — better — make it deterministic: force the interleaving through the existing lock (hold the write lock from the test, assert the second process blocks and then observes the first process's write) so the assertion is a mutual-exclusion invariant rather than a sampling exercise.

finding: "Every guard test surviving §7 has a recorded mutation that makes it fail" names no artifact, no location and no format for the record. It is listed among the tests but it is not a test — nothing runs it, and an auditor in a later round cannot re-derive whether it holds. The one instrument the whole test sweep rests on is the only §12 item with no pass/fail procedure.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 1: the unverifiable mutation record is gone; the marker set is the artifact and the equality is the check.

suggestion: Pin where the mutation record lives and what it contains (e.g. one line per guard test in the closing evidence, or a committed `mutations.ndjson` with {test, file, mutation, observed_failure}), and state the check: the recorded set equals the surviving guard set. If it stays evidence-only prose, move it out of §12 and say explicitly that it is a closure-evidence requirement, not a test.

finding: The governing rule ("a task must be able to name what it removed") is stated as a MUST but is immediately given an unconditioned opt-out ("a task that only adds is not forbidden, but it is the exception and it says so in its evidence") with no criterion for when the exception is legitimate and no enforcement point anywhere in the pipeline. Nothing parses closure evidence: tp done accepts any reason string, the quality gate is a shell command, and §2.3 explicitly says the counts are "not a target". So no artifact distinguishes a compliant task from a non-compliant one — the rule reduces to good faith from exactly the agent §2 says drifts additive. §12's own list makes the exception the norm: items 5, 7, 9, 10 and 11 are new tests and §8.3/§10 are pure additions, so most tasks in the release will invoke the escape hatch. This also runs against the CLAUDE.md rule that a class surviving repeated prose correction gets a check rather than a fourth prose fix.

resolved.evidence: Section 2 no longer claims enforcement tp does not have. It binds decomposition, and every task is declared a removal or a repair in its acceptance.

suggestion: Either name the enforcement point (e.g. a workflow `checks` entry that scans the closing evidence of each task in <base>.tasks.json for a removal line or an explicit `Addition-only:` marker with a stated reason, run every review/audit round), or restate §2 honestly as a decomposition-time rule the human applies when authoring tasks and drop the MUST. Also state the criterion that makes an addition-only task legitimate, so 'it says so in its evidence' is a check rather than a formality.

finding: §3 calls the import write "the last lock-free write path in the tool", but tp init also writes a <base>.tasks.json outside any lock (init.go: a stat guard, then model.WriteTaskFile, no engine.WithFileLock), and tp add --spec reaches that same path by calling runInit before it takes its own lock. After the §3 fix the release still ships a lock-free task-file write with a TOCTOU guard, so the mutual-exclusion promise of §1 is not actually delivered and an implementer following §3 literally builds the wrong scope.

resolved.evidence: Section 3 now names both unlocked writers, importcmd.go and init.go reached via runInit from tp add --spec, and brings both inside WithFileLock.

suggestion: Either bring the init write inside WithFileLock in the same task (and drop the 'last lock-free write path' claim in favour of naming both sites), or state explicitly that init is out of scope and why the stat-then-write race there is acceptable. Whichever way, §3 must enumerate the remaining unlocked task-file writers instead of asserting there are none.

finding: §3 says import honours the resolved `lock_timeout_seconds` and then that there are "no flag and no output changes", while §12 item 2 requires a test that import "fails with the documented exit code when the lock is held". The spec never names that code, and tp's scheme makes 3 (file) and 4 (state) both defensible for a lock timeout — so the test cannot be written from the spec. The two statements also conflict: a lock-timeout failure is a new observable output that import could not previously produce.

resolved.evidence: Section 3 names exit 4 (ExitState) with LockTimeoutError's hint, matching root.go, and limits the no-output-change claim to the success path.

suggestion: Name the exit code and the error/hint shape for a lock timeout in §3 (matching whatever the other write commands already return, stated as a literal), and amend "no output changes" to "no output changes on the success path; a lock timeout adds the same failure output every other write command emits".

finding: §5 changes only the project gate and §12 item 5 asserts only "the resolved project quality gate contains -race", but a task file's own `quality_gate` override wins over the project layer under the v0.24.0 resolution precedence, and `quality_gate` is init-authored and read-only at the task level (`tp set --workflow` rejects it — v0.26.0 §6.1). This repo's spec/0.34.0.tasks.json carries `"quality_gate": "go test ./... && golangci-lint run"` in its own workflow block, so as specified every close in v0.34.0 — and in v0.35.0's unattended run, whose task file will be init-authored the same way — runs the gate WITHOUT -race while the guard test passes. The section's own claim ("the quality gate sees data races") is therefore false for the closes that matter, and the spec never says how an already-authored, non-settable override is changed, given §11.3 forbids new flags and hand-editing <base>.tasks.json is fenced off for units.

resolved.evidence: Section 5 states the requirement on the resolved gate for every spec/*.tasks.json and removes the redundant task-level quality_gate overrides that mask it.

suggestion: State which layer the change targets and how the masking overrides are handled: either the guard test asserts the gate *resolved for tp's own task files* (not just the project default), or §5 names the removal of the redundant `quality_gate` override from spec/*.tasks.json (a subtraction that fits §2 and mirrors the v0.26.0 thinning migration) so the project value is the one that resolves. Say explicitly whether `tp init` for v0.35.0 is expected to author the -race gate, and who is allowed to make the edit.

finding: Enabling `dupl` in `.golangci.yml` changes the shared quality gate, which runs at every `tp done`/`tp close`. If the enabling and the merge/exempt work are decomposed into separate tasks, the enabling task's own close is red the moment dupl reports its first clone, and every later task in the release inherits a red gate until the last clone is resolved. This is exactly the v0.31.2 lesson recorded in CLAUDE.md ("a change and the test it invalidates belong to the SAME task; the gate runs at every tp done, so 'a later task fixes that test' is impossible"), applied to a linter instead of a test. §6.1 states the enabling and the resolution in one sentence but never states that they are one task, and the number of clones is unknown until the detector runs — so the decomposer cannot even size the task.

resolved.evidence: Section 6.1 makes enabling dupl and bringing the tree clean under it one task, with acceptance stated as a clean golangci-lint run rather than a merge count.

suggestion: State the ordering constraint explicitly: enabling `dupl` and bringing the tree to a clean `golangci-lint run` under it are one task (or the enabling task sets the threshold such that the tree is already clean and each subsequent merge lowers it). Note that clone count is discovered, not planned, and say what the unit does if the clean-up exceeds one task — e.g. land the merges first with dupl run manually, and enable it in the gate only in the final task.

finding: §7.1 scopes the sweep to 'every test in the guard class — tests written to prevent a specific defect from returning — plus any test a removal decision depends on', with a manual break/run/restore per test. There is no mechanical way to identify that class: the repo holds ~1100 test functions across ~190 files, guard tests are not marked, and 'a test written to prevent a defect from returning' describes most of them. The implementer cannot size the work, cannot tell when §7 is finished, and cannot split it into one-commit atomic tasks — yet §12.1 says the removals 'are enumerated in their own tasks', which presupposes an enumeration the spec never produces.

resolved.evidence: Section 7.1 replaces the description with a fixed list produced by the release's first task: guard tests added during the v0.31.2 through v0.33.0 audits, named file:function.

suggestion: Make the class enumerable before the sweep starts: define it as an explicit, spec-authored list (e.g. the guard tests added by the v0.31.2–v0.33.0 audit rounds, named file:function), or as tests carrying a marker comment, and cap the sweep at that list. A first task can produce the list as its only deliverable; the mutation tasks then have a countable scope and a checkable done condition.

finding: The sweep's scope is "every test in the guard class — tests written to prevent a specific defect from returning", but nothing in the repo or the spec makes that class enumerable. Authorial intent is not an observable property of a test: on one reading every regression test in the suite qualifies (nearly all tests are written because something broke), on another only the handful named in v0.33.0's audit does. Two engineers therefore sweep different sets, and §12 item 11 ("every guard test surviving §7") has an undefined denominator, so nobody can tell whether the item passed.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 9, plus a // guard: marker on each surviving guard so the class is mechanically enumerable afterwards.

suggestion: Pin the class mechanically before the sweep starts: either enumerate the guard tests by name in the spec/task acceptance, or define a marker the tests must carry (e.g. a `// guard: <defect>` comment or a `TestGuard_*` naming rule) and make §12 item 11 assert over exactly the marked set. State that a test outside the marked set is out of §7.1's scope.

finding: The canonical-home table assigns ownership topically (README owns the command surface and flag inventory; SKILL.md owns how an agent runs a cycle) and then cuts duplicates from the non-owner down to "a one-line summary and a pointer". For a human maintainer that removes drift; for an agent it can increase total reading. SKILL.md is the document an agent actually has loaded while running a cycle, and README is one it typically never opens — so replacing SKILL.md's command/flag detail with a pointer converts a zero-cost in-context lookup into a new file read per lookup. A release whose stated point is that every removed line is a line the loop never has to read would then have added round-trips to the loop.

resolved.evidence: Section 8.1 states the economy rule: the canonical home is the document the actor already has loaded. The ownership table and the checked flag inventory moved to SKILL.md accordingly.

suggestion: State the economy rule that selects the owner: the canonical home is the document the actor performing that task already has loaded, and pointers must run from the rarely-loaded document to the always-loaded one, never the reverse. Concretely, keep the flags and command forms an agent needs mid-cycle inline in SKILL.md and let README point at it, rather than the other way round; reserve the pointer-only treatment for facts (exhaustive schema, exit-code tables) that are looked up rarely and belong in the Reference.

finding: The documented recipe compares models by running the same reviewer role "in one round on one model and in another round on a second model, then reading unique". The two rounds do not see the same spec: round N+1 reviews a document already repaired against round N's findings, so a low unique count for the second model is indistinguishable from "the first round already removed the findings it would have made". The recipe therefore costs a full extra review round per role under test and returns a number that cannot support the decision it is documented to support.
suggestion: Either specify the only design that isolates the model axis — both models run the same role against the same unrepaired spec revision within one round, then compare unique — or document the confound explicitly and mark the reading as directional only. If same-round dual-model fan-out is out of reach, say so and drop the recipe rather than shipping a measurement whose cost is a round and whose result is uninterpretable.

finding: The recipe reads `unique` for one role across two rounds run on two models, but `overlap_report` is a within-round, across-role instrument, and consecutive review rounds are not comparable: the spec text changes between rounds, findings resolved in round N cannot recur in round N+1, and the panel composition differs. A `unique` delta measured this way confounds model diversity with spec repair and round position. Nothing in the recorded finding rows carries the model either, so the attribution lives only in someone's memory of which round used which model. "No feature changes; the instrument exists and the axis was simply never named" therefore overstates what the existing instrument supports.
suggestion: Either state the controlled procedure that makes the comparison valid — same spec revision, same round, the same role run twice under two models as two distinct role ids so `overlap_report` compares them within one round — or document it honestly as an indicative measurement with the confounds named. If model attribution is needed to make the number readable, that is a feature and belongs in a later version, not in a documentation-only section.

finding: Non-Goal 2 says the deferred `scope`/`audit_converge_on` work is "still carried in spec/0.34.0-candidates.md", but the repo convention names a candidates file for the *upcoming* version — spec/0.33.0-candidates.md carries what the v0.32.0 cycle deferred, and CLAUDE.md instructs the next cycle to read the file named for the version it is about to write. spec/0.34.0-candidates.md is the file the v0.33.0 cycle wrote to feed *this* release; leaving a twice-deferred item there means the v0.35.0 cycle, which reads spec/0.35.0-candidates.md, never sees it. For an item already deferred twice and headed into an unattended release, that is how a deferral is lost rather than carried.
suggestion: Point Non-Goal 2 at spec/0.35.0-candidates.md and make authoring/updating that file part of this release (it is also the home for the §8.1 CLAUDE.md rules named for v0.36.0 mechanization, which currently have no artifact either).

finding: "The three write defects are the only intentional behaviour changes in this release" is contradicted by §9: §9.1 changes an unknown command from exit 1 to exit 2, and §9.2/§9.3 change hint text users and drivers read. §12 item 6 compounds this by requiring "existing exit codes are unchanged" in the same breath as §4 changes an over-cap bulk line from exit 0 to exit 3 and §9.1 changes 1 to 2. A test writer cannot tell which exit codes are in the "unchanged" set, and there is no enumerated inventory to diff against.

resolved.evidence: Non-Goal 1 rewritten to enumerate all five intentional behaviour changes.

suggestion: Restate non-goal 1 as "no behaviour changes beyond the defects and exit-code/hint corrections named in §3, §4, §5 and §9", and replace §12 item 6's "existing exit codes are unchanged" with an explicit before/after table of the codes that change plus a golden inventory test over the rest.

finding: §12 item 11 — 'Every guard test surviving §7 has a recorded mutation that makes it fail' — is listed as a test but is not one: nothing in the suite can assert it, and the spec never says where the record lives (a comment above the test, the closure evidence of the §7 task, a file under .tp-review/, the release notes). Two tasks reading this item would produce two incompatible artifacts, and a later reader has no place to look to verify the claim.

resolved.evidence: Test item 11 replaced with an equality over the // guard: marker set, which is a real oracle.

suggestion: Move item 11 out of the test list into §7.1 as a documentation obligation, and name the artifact and its format — e.g. each surviving guard test gains a one-line 'mutation: <what was broken> -> <this test fails>' comment, and the closing evidence names the count. If it stays in §12, say which automated check enforces it.

finding: The removal contract requires every removal to name its surviving coverage in the closing evidence, and §2 requires even add-only tasks to say so in evidence. Closure evidence is not write-only: it lands in closed_reason and commit bodies, and tp's own brief injects each dependency's evidence into every downstream unit's context. In a release built almost entirely of removal tasks, that makes justification prose the dominant term in later briefs, and no bound or shape is given for it — so the rule's cost scales with dependents, not with removals.
suggestion: Bound the evidence: one line per removal in a fixed shape (removed <thing> — covered by <test/function/document>), with rationale left to the commit body rather than closed_reason. If a removal needs more than that, it is a design change and belongs under non-goal 7 rather than in an evidence paragraph every dependent re-reads.

finding: The Code row offers two evidence forms — "it had no caller" or "the single remaining implementation that absorbed it" — and neither fits §6.3, where whole branches are removed. A branch has no caller, and nothing absorbs it; the evidence would have to be an unreachability argument, and the spec gives no standard for one (type-system exclusion? coverage report? exhaustive switch?). The removal contract is also the governing rule of the release and no §12 item verifies compliance with it, so a task can close having named nothing.
suggestion: Add a fourth row for a removed branch stating the accepted evidence (e.g. the type or switch that excludes the state, or a coverage run showing the branch unexecuted), and add a §12 item asserting that every closing evidence for a removal task contains a naming line in the contract's shape.

finding: §2.3 asks the release notes to carry before-and-after counts for five quantities while §2.2 has just declared that line count and test count are not the metric and §2.3 itself says the numbers are not a target. Four of the five are cheap to derive, but "the number of documented facts that had more than one home" is a judgment pass over four documents that must be performed twice — once before the sweep, on a state that stops existing the moment the sweep starts. The most expensive measurement in the release feeds no decision inside the release.
suggestion: Keep only the counts a command can produce (source lines, test count, exported symbols, documentation lines) and record them as a one-line snapshot taken before the first sweep task. Replace the duplicated-fact count with the artifact that actually pays for itself: the list of facts the sweep relocated and their new home, which the §8.2/§8.3 equality tests then keep honest.

finding: Five before-and-after counts are required with no counting rule for any of them: "source lines" (blank/comment lines? are `_test.go` files source?), "test count" (top-level Test functions, subtests, or table cases?), "exported symbols" (across `internal/`, where everything is effectively package-private?), "documentation lines" (which files?), and "the number of documented facts that had more than one home" (no enumeration procedure exists anywhere in the spec). Two engineers produce five different pairs of numbers, so the recorded fact cannot be compared against the next cycle's — which is the entire stated purpose.
location: §2.3 The release records what it removed
suggestion: Pin each count as a command whose output is the number (e.g. a `scripts/` one-liner or an explicit `find`/`go doc` recipe committed with the release), and drop or redefine the "facts with more than one home" count once §8.1 defines an enumerable unit.

finding: §3 promises "No flag and no output changes", but §12 item 2 requires `tp import` to "fail with the documented exit code when the lock is held" — a failure path, error message and hint that import does not have today, i.e. an output change. The item also never names the exit code ("the documented exit code"), and the spec's own §9 is dedicated to exit-code consistency, so leaving the one new failure classification implicit is the gap that section exists to close. An implementer reading §3 and a tester reading item 2 build different things.

resolved.evidence: Section 3 limits the no-output-change claim to the success path and names exit 4 with LockTimeoutError's hint for the failure path.

suggestion: Restrict §3's promise to the success path ("no flag changes and no change to successful output") and state the lock-timeout failure explicitly: the exit code (matching what every other write command emits on lock-acquisition timeout), the message, and the hint naming the task file.

finding: §3 says the import move honours the resolved lock_timeout_seconds yet also says 'No flag and no output changes', while §12 item 2 requires a test that import 'fails with the documented exit code when the lock is held' without naming that code or its hint. Import has no lock-contention failure mode today, so this IS a new observable output: a new error object, a new exit code and a new hint. The implementer has to infer both the code and whether the new failure contradicts the no-output-change sentence and the §11 item 1 non-goal.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 21: the lock-timeout error path is now specified.

suggestion: Name the failure explicitly: on contention past lock_timeout_seconds, tp import exits 4 (STATE) with engine.LockTimeoutError's message and hint, the same as every other locked writer. Reword 'No flag and no output changes' to 'no changes to the success output; the only new output is the exit-4 contention error', and list it as an intentional behaviour change in §11 item 1.

finding: §4 classifies an over-cap line as exit 3 (file), while §9.1 argues in the same release that tp must classify failures by the documented scheme (0=success, 1=validation, 2=usage, 3=file). A line that exceeds a cap in a file that opened and read fine is on its face a validation error (1), not a file error (3); the only justification given is precedent from the v0.33.0 review/audit sweep. Either the precedent is right and the reasoning should be stated, or §9's own standard says the shared cap is misclassified — and a driver that classifies failures by exit code (the reason §9.1 gives for changing unknown-command to 2) cannot tell an unreadable file from an over-long line.
suggestion: State the classification rationale in §4 — e.g. the cap is a reader-level limit, so a file tp declines to read is a file error and the whole shared-cap family stays 3 — so the choice is a recorded decision rather than an unexplained divergence from §9's standard. If instead the family should be 1, say so and scope the change.

finding: §4 generalises the fix into a rule — 'a bulk operation either applies every row or applies none' — but tp set --bulk today deliberately reports per-row partial success (a results array with per-line error strings and updated/failed counts, and it still writes the file), and tp done --batch has the same closed/failed contract. Read as written, the sentence orders the removal of documented partial-success semantics; read narrowly, it applies only to the over-cap abort. §11 item 1 forbids behaviour changes outside the named defects, so the two readings differ by a large, user-visible change.
suggestion: Scope the sentence to the cap: 'an over-cap line aborts before any write; per-row failures (unknown id, managed field, invalid JSON) keep their existing partial-success reporting unchanged.' If the all-or-nothing rule is meant to cover row-level failures too, that is a second defect and needs its own row in §1 and its own test in §12.

finding: The gate becomes go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run and §12.1 accepts that this roughly doubles suite wall time. The gate runs on every tp done, so the cost multiplies by the task count of a release made of many small removal tasks, and v0.35.0's unattended run inherits it. The spec never checks the doubled duration against the resolved gate_timeout_seconds (default 600, max 3600): if the current suite sits anywhere near half that, every close starts timing out and each one costs a failed gate plus a retry.
suggestion: Record the measured gate duration before and after -race in §5, and state whether the resolved gate_timeout_seconds still covers it with margin — raising the project default in the same task if it does not. That number is also the honest input to the -race recommendation §5 makes to other projects.

finding: §5 states that `-race` "roughly doubles test wall time" but never revisits `gate_timeout_seconds`, the resolved workflow field (default 600, range 30-3600) that bounds the gate at every `tp done`/`tp close`. If the current suite runs anywhere near half the resolved timeout, the release makes every close fail on timeout — a failure mode that looks like a red gate and would be debugged as one, and that lands hardest in v0.35.0's unattended run where nobody is watching. The spec measures the cost in prose and then does not act on the one knob that the cost interacts with.
suggestion: State the measured before/after wall time of `go test ./...` versus `go test -race ./...` on this tree, and either confirm the resolved `gate_timeout_seconds` still has headroom or raise the project default in the same task as the gate change (and pin it in the same config-assertion guard test).

finding: "The resolved project quality gate" does not identify what the guard test resolves against. `quality_gate` is init-authored per task file and tp's own repo carries several `spec/*.tasks.json`; resolution is layered (CLI > env > task > project > built-in). One engineer asserts the value in `.tp/config.json`, another asserts the resolved value for the active task file, a third asserts it for every task file in the repo — and only the third catches a stale per-file override masking the new project default.
location: §5 The quality gate sees data races

resolved.evidence: Section 5 states the requirement on the gate resolved for every spec/*.tasks.json, not on the project layer.

suggestion: Say which layer and which files the guard covers, e.g. "the project default in `.tp/config.json` equals the literal gate, and no `spec/*.tasks.json` carries a `quality_gate` override" — both halves as separate assertions.

finding: §5 requires the gate to become `go test -race ./... && golangci-lint run`, but §12 item 5 only asserts the resolved gate "contains `-race`". A gate edited down to `go test -race ./...` — dropping golangci-lint entirely — passes that assertion. That is precisely the "gate weakened by an edit should fail a test" failure the section invokes v0.31.1 to prevent, so the stated assertion does not enforce the stated requirement.
location: §5 The quality gate sees data races

resolved.evidence: Test item 5 now asserts equality with the exact gate string instead of a contains check.

suggestion: State the assertion as string equality against the full literal gate command, and quote that literal once in §5 so the test transcribes it rather than paraphrasing it.

finding: The `dupl` threshold is specified as "tuned against the current tree" so that "the initial report is small enough to act on", with the stated failure mode being a detector that reports a hundred findings and gets disabled. Neither bound is measurable, and the incentives point the wrong way: a unit satisfies §6.1 completely by choosing a threshold high enough that dupl reports nothing, shipping a permanently green detector that removes nothing — in a release whose governing rule is that every task names what it removed. The section also interacts with Non-Goal 7 (a merge needing a new abstraction is out of scope), so the residue is `nolint` exemptions, i.e. text added by a subtraction release.

resolved.evidence: Section 6.1 pins the threshold: dupl's own default, raised only to the lowest value at which the tree is clean, recorded in .golangci.yml with the reason.

suggestion: Pin the acceptance in measurable terms: state the threshold value chosen (or the procedure and the target report size, e.g. 'the largest threshold that still reports the two-readers and two-prompt-builders clones named in this section'), and require the task's evidence to name each reported clone and its disposition (merged, or exempted with the reason). That way the section's success is the dispositions, not the setting.

finding: §6.1 requires dupl 'at a threshold tuned against the current tree' with the stop condition 'the initial report is small enough to act on'. No number is given, and nothing says whether _test.go files are in scope — golangci-lint analyses test files by default, and this repo has ~190 test files built from near-identical fixture blocks, so the default run is exactly the hundred-finding report the section says gets a detector disabled. The implementer must invent both the threshold and the definition of done, and no reviewer can check the task closed correctly.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 29: the acceptance is the recorded threshold plus a clean run.

suggestion: Pin the concrete configuration in the spec: the dupl threshold value, whether run.tests is false for it (or dupl is excluded on _test.go via issues.exclude-rules), and an acceptance the task can be closed against — e.g. 'the enabled configuration reports at most N clones on the current tree, and each is merged or carries a //nolint:dupl with a one-line reason'.

finding: The `dupl` threshold is specified only as "tuned against the current tree" and "chosen so the initial report is small enough to act on", with the failure mode illustrated by "a hundred findings". No number, no bound, no acceptance criterion — and there is no §12 item covering §6 at all, so nothing in the test list observes whether the detector was enabled, what it was set to, or whether the exemptions carry reasons. A later reader cannot tell a tuned threshold from one raised until the report was empty.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 29.

suggestion: Either pin the threshold (or a bound such as "the largest threshold whose report is under N clones", with N stated) and record the chosen value with the resulting clone count in the closing evidence, and add a §12 item asserting `dupl` is enabled in `.golangci.yml` at that value and that the gate passes with every remaining clone carrying an inline exemption reason.

finding: Test 11 in §12 requires that "every guard test surviving §7 has a recorded mutation that makes it fail", but §7.1 defines the mutation procedure as manual and never says where the record lives or what shape it has. As written this is either a new per-test annotation that every future guard test must carry — a recurring authoring and reading cost, and a new surface in a release whose non-goal 3 forbids new surface and whose non-goal 4 defers mutation tooling to v0.36.0 — or it is not a test at all and cannot appear in the test list.

resolved.evidence: The mutation record is gone; section 7.1 keeps the procedure and the // guard: marker is the artifact.

suggestion: Pin the record to an existing surface and a fixed shape: one comment line above the guard test naming the mutation and the observed failure (mutation: <change> -> <test> fails), asserted by nothing. Then restate item 11 as a checklist obligation of the §7 tasks rather than a test, so the test list keeps only claims a run of go test can decide.

finding: The keep/delete decision turns on two undefined terms. "The same path" is never defined — same public command, same internal function, same code branch? — yet it is the sole discriminator between "duplication, delete" and "coverage, keep". And the survivor is "the one whose failure message identifies the defect best", a superlative with no criterion; two engineers keep different tests and delete each other's keepers. Deletion is the irreversible direction, so the ambiguity is asymmetric.
suggestion: Define "same path" concretely (e.g. same entry point AND same code branch under test, judged by the covered lines), and replace "identifies the defect best" with an ordered tiebreak (e.g. prefer the test whose name and failure message name the defect; then the one exercising the public command over an internal helper).

finding: The protection list covers §8's equality tests, §5's config guard and any test guarding a silent-write defect — but not §9's hint tests, which the same release is expanding. `TestFileErrorsCarryAHint` and the §12.8 `specFileMissingHint` test assert exact hint strings, which is verbatim §7.3's removable class ("an exact log string"). One task adds them, another may convert or delete them, and both cite the spec. "Any test whose failure would let a silent-write defect return" is also an undefined class — no definition of "silent-write defect" is given.
location: §7.4 What the sweep must not touch
suggestion: Add the §9 hint tests to §7.4's protected list explicitly, and carve exact-string assertions out of §7.3 when the string is the documented contract (a hint the user reads) rather than an internal log line. Define or drop the "silent-write defect" phrase in favour of naming the tests.

finding: "CLAUDE.md ... has accreted rules that are not about this repository at all — those either move to SKILL.md, where every user gets them" treats SKILL.md as free space. It is not: SKILL.md is loaded into the context of every agent that invokes the tp skill, so each rule relocated there is a permanent per-session token charge on every tp user, paid to carry lessons derived from tp's own development. The sweep gives no criterion for which of those rules earn that charge, so the default outcome is that all of them move and the always-loaded footprint grows in a subtraction release.
suggestion: Add an admission test for SKILL.md: a rule moves there only if it changes what an agent does during a cycle it will plausibly run (decomposition, gate, close recipe). Rules that are post-mortems, rationale, or single-project history go to the Reference (or are dropped once mechanized), and record the before/after SKILL.md size alongside the other counts in §2.3 so the charge is visible.

finding: The ownership table treats the four documents as interchangeable homes distinguished only by topic, but CLAUDE.md and SKILL.md have different loading semantics: CLAUDE.md is injected into every agent's context automatically, while skills/tp/SKILL.md is loaded on demand via the Skill tool. Moving a load-bearing self-development rule from CLAUDE.md to SKILL.md changes whether the agent driving the loop sees it at all — and §1 schedules this release immediately before the unattended v0.35.0 run, where an unseen rule is unrecoverable. §8.1 also silently invalidates CLAUDE.md's own pre-release checklist, which requires README.md, CLAUDE.md and SKILL.md to each reflect every new command, flag and workflow change; under one-canonical-home that checklist item becomes wrong, and the spec never says it is updated.

resolved.evidence: The ownership table gains a Loaded by column and the economy rule that selects the owner.

suggestion: Add the loading-semantics constraint to §8.1: a rule may move out of CLAUDE.md only if it is not needed by an agent that has not loaded the tp skill, otherwise it stays with a pointer in the other direction. Name the CLAUDE.md pre-release checklist as one of the facts this sweep rewrites, so the checklist ends up asserting 'each document owns its part' rather than 'all three repeat everything'.

finding: §8.1 requires each fact to have one home and "anything duplicated across two homes is cut from the non-owner", but §5 in the same release mandates that both README.md and skills/tp/SKILL.md recommend `-race` — the same fact in two homes. The four-row ownership table also assigns no owner for recommendations/workflow policy of this kind (README owns "what tp is, install, the command surface, the flag inventory"; SKILL.md owns "how an agent runs a cycle"). A task implementing §8.1 cannot decide whether the §5 recommendation is a violation to cut or an exception to keep.

resolved.evidence: Section 5's -race recommendation now has one home, skills/tp/SKILL.md, so it no longer contradicts section 8.1.

suggestion: Either add an explicit exception clause ("a pointer or a one-line summary at a non-owner is not duplication; a second full statement is") and classify the -race recommendation under it, or name the single owner of cross-project recommendations in the §8.1 table and have the other document point at it.

finding: §8.2 and §8.3 each get an equality test precisely because "a prose table that nothing checks will drift again", yet §8.1 — the rule that governs both, and the largest edit in the release — gets no check at all and no §12 item. "A fact" is also never defined operationally: is a duplicated flag name a fact, a duplicated sentence, a duplicated concept? Without an enumeration procedure there is no way to verify that duplication was cut, nor to re-verify it in a later round.
suggestion: Add a §12 item with a mechanical proxy for §8.1 — e.g. a check that no non-owner document contains more than a one-line summary plus a pointer for a set of enumerated topics, or at minimum a committed list of the facts that were de-duplicated with their new home — and define "fact" as the unit that list uses.

finding: 'A test asserts the documented rule set equals the engine's rule set' has no source of truth on either side. The engine has no rule registry: Rule strings are literals scattered across lint_rules.go, vague.go, frontmatter.go and structured.go, and the SAME Finding.Rule namespace is also used by the non-lint paths (validate.go emits schema/atomicity/coverage/section-anchor, linecoverage.go emits line-coverage, entry.go emits id-blank/title-blank/…). §8.2's own 'absent' list crosses that boundary by naming section-anchor, which validate.go emits, so the implementer must first decide what counts as a lint rule and then invent a way to enumerate it. The README side is equally unspecified — no machine-readable form for the table is named.

resolved.evidence: Section 8.2 states that the engine gains an exported enumeration of its lint rule identifiers as the source for the engine side of the equality.

suggestion: State both sides: add (or name) a single exported enumeration in the engine that every lint emitter draws its Rule from, say explicitly whether tp validate's rules are in or out of the table, and specify the README form the test parses (e.g. the first column of the fenced rule table, one rule per row).

finding: The section's own numbers do not reconcile: 9 documented rules plus the 8 named as absent is 17, not "about 20". Either the absent list is not exhaustive (in which case the task cannot know which rules it must document and the equality test's target set is unpinned before implementation), or it is exhaustive and "about 20" is wrong. "About" is also the wrong register for a section whose whole point is that the table is complete and stays complete.

resolved.evidence: The exact count is settled by that enumeration rather than by the spec's approximation.

suggestion: State the exact engine rule count and either list every absent rule or say explicitly that the list is illustrative and the task derives the set from the engine. The equality test of §12 item 9 is the arbiter, so the spec only needs to name the source of truth — but the two figures it does give must agree.

finding: The test must compare two exact sets, but the spec pins neither. The engine side is "about 20" rules — an approximation, and it does not reconcile with the section's own arithmetic (9 documented plus the 8 named as absent is 17), so a task cannot tell whether the list of absent rules is complete or three rules short. The document side has no extraction contract (which table, which column, what identifies a rule id). "With one line each" is likewise unmeasurable — one line of what?
location: §8.2 The lint rule table is complete and stays complete

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 39: both sides of the equality now have a stated source.

suggestion: Replace "about 20" with the exact rule-id set (or state that the task derives it from the engine and commits it as the golden list), specify the table's machine-readable shape (rule id in a code span in column 1, description in column 2), and define the per-rule line requirement as "a non-empty description cell".

finding: 'the flag inventory gains the same equality test as the lint rules' does not define either set. The CLI side is ambiguous between bare flag names and (command, flag) pairs — --force exists on init, import and review with different meanings, and the persistent root flags belong to every command — and the spec does not say whether shorthands, hidden or deprecated flags count. The README side has no machine-readable inventory today; flags appear inside prose and code fences, so a naive '--token' scrape picks up flags mentioned in explanations and misses those only shown in examples.

resolved.evidence: Section 8.3 states both sets: every flag registered on any command with persistent flags counted once, against the inventory in skills/tp/SKILL.md.

suggestion: Specify the key ((command, long-flag) pairs, root persistent flags listed once), what is excluded (shorthands, --help/--version), and the README structure the test parses — e.g. a per-command flag table whose rows the test reads, so the test fails on a missing row rather than on prose wording.

finding: "The documented flag inventory equals the flags the CLI defines" has no set boundary on either side. On the CLI side: are persistent/global flags counted once or once per command that inherits them; are shorthands separate entries; are hidden, deprecated and auto-generated flags (`--help`, `--version`) in or out; do the negated forms (`--no-compact`, `--no-color`, `--no-quiet`) count as distinct flags? On the document side, no extraction rule is given for how the inventory is parsed out of Markdown. Two engineers write equality tests that disagree on dozens of entries.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 42.

suggestion: State the inventory's unit (e.g. `command + long flag name`, negated forms listed with their positive form, `--help`/`--version` excluded, hidden flags excluded) and the machine-readable shape the document must use (e.g. one table row per flag with the name in a code span) so the test's parse is defined rather than inferred.

finding: Unknown commands, unknown subcommands and wrong-argument-count errors all arrive at the same place — the single err branch in root.go's Execute, after the typed flagUsageError and LockTimeoutError checks — and cobra gives no typed error for any of them. §9.1 classifies only unknown commands, so the implementer must decide unaided what happens to the sibling cases that the obvious fix (treating cobra's pre-run errors as usage errors) sweeps in, while §12 item 6 simultaneously demands 'existing exit codes are unchanged'. Separately, 'unknown subcommands' has no referent: every tp command is a direct child of root, so tp has no nested subcommand to get wrong, and that half of item 6 cannot be tested.
suggestion: Enumerate the cobra error classes and the code each carries: unknown command -> 2, and state explicitly whether arg-count errors ('accepts 1 arg(s), received 2') stay at 1 or move to 2. Drop the 'unknown subcommand' clause, or add the concrete case meant (e.g. an extra positional to a zero-arg command such as tp config) so §12 item 6 has something to assert.

finding: §12 item 7 states the guard as 'Each ExitValidation site carries a hint naming the file that site operates on', but many validation sites have no file as their object: an invalid review_converge_on value, 'review not converged', 'finding N already resolved', and tp set --local's flag-syntax errors all raise ExitValidation about a config value or a state, not a path. Taken literally the guard forces a wrong hint onto those sites. Worse, the site §9.2 actually names — root.go's generic fallback, which reports any RunE-returned error as ExitValidation with no hint — cannot name a file at all, is not in taskFileCommands, and is untouched by a per-call-site remedy, so extending the guard flags it with no correct repair available.
suggestion: Restate the criterion as the ExitFile guard already works — a non-empty, site-appropriate hint, with a marker comment where the code-1 task-file default really is the right advice — rather than 'names the file'. Then say what happens to root.go's fallback: either give it a hint that names no file, or exempt it by name with the reason recorded, the way taskFileCommands records its entries.

finding: §9.2 requires validation errors from commands "whose object is not the task file" to carry a hint naming their own object, and §12 item 7 turns that into an enumeration: "Each ExitValidation site carries a hint naming the file that site operates on." Many ExitValidation sites have no file object at all — a rejected managed field in `tp set`, a one-word closure reason in `tp done`, `tp add`'s entry-rule validation, an out-of-range `tp set --workflow` value. As written the enumerating test cannot be satisfied for those sites, and a unit will either invent a file for them or quietly exempt them, which is the silent-exemption pattern §9.3 is fixing elsewhere in this same spec.
suggestion: Define the contract over hint *objects*, not files: every ExitValidation site carries a hint naming the object it validated (a file and line where one exists, otherwise the field, flag or argument), and the enumerating test asserts a non-default hint per site rather than a filename. Say what the default-hint sites become, so the enumeration has no unstated exemptions.

finding: §9.2 scopes the change to "validation errors raised by commands whose object is not the task file", while §12 item 7 requires that "each `ExitValidation` site carries a hint naming the file that site operates on". These are different sets, and the second is not satisfiable: many validation errors have no file object at all (an invalid field value in `tp set`, a mutually exclusive flag combination, a bad range on a workflow field). A test enumerating every site will fail on those, and the spec does not say what hint they should carry.
suggestion: Align the two: state the predicate once (e.g. "every `ExitValidation` site whose error concerns a file names that file; sites with no file object carry a hint naming the field or flag at fault") and have §12 item 7 assert exactly that partition, with the file-less category enumerated so the test can classify.

finding: 'They adopt specFileMissingHint and leave the list' understates the change, because leaving taskFileCommands puts EVERY hintless exit-3 site in those two files under the guard, not only the spec-path ones. init.go's exit-3 sites include 'task file already exists' (where the code-3 task-file default is the correct advice), the task-file write failure, the .tp directory MkdirAll/gitignore failures, and the --eject-roles corpus sites; lint.go's include a JSON-encode failure that wants internalEncodeHint. Applied literally the sentence produces hints that name a spec path for errors that have nothing to do with the spec.
suggestion: Say per site class what each gets: the spec-read sites take specFileMissingHint, the encode site takes internalEncodeHint, the .tp/role-corpus sites take their own hint, and 'task file already exists' keeps the code-3 default marked with a task-file-hint: comment. That also makes the task's acceptance checkable against the guard rather than against a one-line summary.

finding: 'The recipe is documented in its canonical home' names no document, in the release that makes 'canonical home' a defined term. Under the §8.1 table the model-diversity recipe could plausibly land in skills/tp/SKILL.md (how an agent runs a cycle) or CLAUDE.md (this repository's own self-development loop), and §10.1 by contrast names skills/tp/SKILL.md outright. The implementer has to guess, and a wrong guess is exactly the duplication §8.1 exists to remove.

resolved.evidence: The recipe's home is named: skills/tp/SKILL.md.

suggestion: Name the file, as §10.1 does, and say which document (if any) carries the one-line summary and pointer.

finding: "and so does the second reader implementation if the two turn out to be the same code twice" makes part of the section's outcome conditional on a discovery, so a task's acceptance cannot be pinned before the work starts and its closing evidence has a legitimate 'the condition did not hold' answer that nothing can check. Non-Goal 7 further constrains the merge (if it needs a new abstraction it is out of scope), so there are two escape hatches on the one removal §4 actually promises.
suggestion: Split the discovery from the commitment: state the removal that is unconditional (the `line-cap:` markers and the warn-and-continue paths), and record the reader-unification as a separate decision whose outcome — merged, or kept with the reason the two are not the same code — is required in the evidence either way.

finding: The new bulk failure mode aborts "naming the file and the line number" — singular. A bulk file authored by an agent can contain several over-cap lines, and a first-offender-only message turns repair into one edit and one rerun per bad line. Since the operation now writes nothing, the scan is free: every offending line is already discoverable in the pass that found the first.
suggestion: Have the abort report every over-cap line found in the scan (file plus the full line-number list, capped at a small number with a count of the remainder), so a bulk file with N bad rows is repaired in one round trip. If matching the review/audit family's shared failure mode forbids this, say so in §4 and note the round-trip cost as a deliberate consistency trade.

finding: "...and so does the second reader implementation if the two turn out to be the same code twice" is a conditional removal with no test for the condition. "The same code twice" has no threshold (identical? same contract, different formatting? whatever `dupl` flags at the §6.1 threshold?), so a task's acceptance cannot state a verifiable outcome — both merging and not merging satisfy the sentence.
location: §4 The bulk readers honour the shared line cap
suggestion: State the decision procedure and its evidence: e.g. "if `dupl` at the §6.1 threshold reports the two readers as a clone, they merge into one function and the closing evidence names it; otherwise the evidence names the behavioural difference that keeps them apart".

finding: §5 puts the `-race` recommendation in both README.md and skills/tp/SKILL.md, while §8.1 of the same spec establishes one canonical home per fact and cuts anything duplicated across two homes from the non-owner. Under the §8.1 table this fact belongs to SKILL.md (how an agent runs a cycle) and not to README.md (what tp is, install, command surface, flag inventory) — or the table needs a row for gate/workflow guidance. As written, one task creates the duplication another task is chartered to remove.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as index 37: one home for the -race recommendation.

suggestion: Name the single home for the -race recommendation and give the other document a one-line pointer, or add the missing ownership category to the §8.1 table if quality-gate guidance genuinely belongs to README.

finding: §5 states that `-race` "roughly doubles test wall time" and §12.1 accepts the slower suite as a cost, but neither addresses `gate_timeout_seconds` (default 600, range 30–3600), which the quality gate is run under at every `tp done`/`tp close`. If the doubled suite crosses the resolved timeout, every close in this release fails for a reason unrelated to the task — and the spec gives no measured before/after wall time to show the headroom exists.
location: §5 The quality gate sees data races
suggestion: Record the measured wall time with and without `-race` in §5, and either state that the resolved `gate_timeout_seconds` already covers it with margin or raise the project default in the same task.

finding: The requirement is expressed purely as internals — "they adopt `specFileMissingHint` and leave the list" (of `taskFileCommands`) — rather than as the observable contract a test asserts. The correctness of "adopted the constant" can only be established by reading code, and a task could satisfy the letter while emitting a hint that names the wrong file. §12 item 8 inherits the same framing.
location: §9.3 `lint` and `init` name the spec, not the task file
suggestion: State the observable outcome first — on a missing spec argument, `tp lint` and `tp init` exit 3 with a hint naming the spec path the user passed — and keep the constant/list mechanics as task acceptance detail rather than the spec's requirement.
